analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering medical, dental, hospital, and nursing care, funded by a new value-added tax.
analysis.headline: Dingell's national health insurance bill never got a hearing or vote: referred to two House committees in January 1997, sent to a health subcommittee on January 23, and left to die with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put the federal government in charge of paying for personal health care — doctor visits, dental care, hospital stays, home nursing, and some prescription drugs — for people who meet work-history requirements, with patients free to choose their own doctors and hospitals. It would have raised the money through a value-added tax on most goods and services, with food, housing, and medical care exempt, and deposited it in a dedicated National Health Care Trust Fund. Administration would have been decentralized to states and local committees. It never advanced past its initial committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and their dependents who would have received medical, dental, hospital, and nursing care without premiums, deductibles, or networks, plus the needy uninsured, whose services could be reimbursed through existing federal grants to states. Retirees and Social Security beneficiaries would qualify, and Medicare beneficiaries could use the program for services Medicare does not cover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and their families needing coverage

how_it_helps.text: Establishes prepaid personal health insurance on a social-insurance principle, making medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services available to eligible individuals nationwide [S2][S3].
Lets every eligible patient freely choose and change their physician, dentist, hospital, or medical group [S2][S3].
Allows services to be furnished to needy individuals not otherwise eligible, paid for through existing federal grants to states under Medicaid and related programs [S2][S3].
Prohibits discrimination by race, creed, or color in providing benefits and in letting qualified providers participate [S3].
Keeps individual health information confidential, with criminal penalties for unauthorized disclosure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and businesses pay a new value-added tax on most sales of goods and services, with the seller liable for remitting it; retail food, principal-residence housing, medical care, and certain government and nonprofit transactions are taxed at zero. Private insurers would lose their current role in paying for basic care, and employers would no longer carry that expense — the tax replaces it.

drawbacks.text: A value-added tax falls on consumption, which weighs more heavily on lower-income households than on the wealthy, even with food and housing exempt [S2].

Coverage is tied to work history — roughly $2,000 in wages over a recent period — or to Social Security or civil-service retirement benefits, so people outside the workforce are covered only if a public agency reimburses the fund for their care [S3].

The National Health Insurance Board may limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services when personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate, and hospital coverage is capped at 60 days a year, with hospitalization for psychosis excluded after 30 days [S2][S3].
Medicare beneficiaries get this program's benefits only for services Medicare does not pay for, rather than a full merger of the two programs, which is deferred to a future study [S2][S3].
Providers may reject patients consistent with state law and professional ethics, so access would depend on where practitioners choose to practice [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a broad, premium-free benefit package with free choice of doctor, which is the core of what private insurance fails to deliver for people without employer coverage. The trade-offs are real: a consumption tax is regressive, eligibility leaves out non-workers, and a Board could ration services when money runs short. It was also a sweeping restructuring that would have displaced the entire private insurance financing system — a cost its supporters accepted and its opponents would not.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced: referred to both the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, sent to the Commerce health subcommittee on January 23, 1997, and never taken up again before the Congress ended — with not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the opening day of the 105th Congress [S1][S5].
The Speaker referred it to the Commerce Committee and additionally to the Ways and Means Committee, because a value-added tax falls under Ways and Means jurisdiction [S3][S5].
On January 23, 1997, it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no markup, hearing, or floor action followed [S5].
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system — private insurers, employers who sponsor coverage, and providers under current payment arrangements — was untouched, because the bill never advanced. The roughly 40 million Americans then uninsured gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent insurers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Insurance Act on the first day of the 105th Congress, carrying forward the long-standing Dingell family national health insurance proposal.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (chaired by a Republican); its Subcommittee on Health and Environment took the referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote after the January 7 referral and January 23 subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (its jurisdiction covered the bill's value-added tax financing)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.role: Nationwide industry whose core business the bill would have replaced
against.what_they_did: Long-standing and widely reported opposition to national health insurance proposals, which would have shifted financing of basic care from private premiums to a government trust fund.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party — the bill stood alone with its Democratic sponsor in a Republican-controlled House, so no partisan alignment was ever tested on the record.

industries.note: The bill would move financing of basic medical care into a government trust fund, eliminating private insurers' role in paying for core coverage, though it permits voluntary health-service organizations to contract with state agencies for service delivery. Insurers' interest in the bill ran against the uninsured and underinsured, who would have gained coverage without premiums.

Hospitals would be paid reasonable cost for covered care from a public fund, ending uncompensated care from the uninsured, but subject to Board-set maximum rates and least-expensive-accommodation defaults. Their existing billing and payment arrangements would be replaced.

Practitioners could bill the program for every eligible patient with free choice of practice locality and pay tied to professional skill and income adequacy, but payment methods (fee schedule, per-capita, or salary) would be set by majority election among area practitioners and rates adapted to public purposes.

Employers' obligation to provide or fund private coverage would effectively disappear for covered care, but the value-added tax is levied on sellers and ultimately passed through to consumers, including workers, as a broad new cost of living.
